tavernInnNames.name: Tavern & Inn Names
items: The Gilded Eel — A canal-side inn whose keeper launders coin for three rival guilds and pretends not to notice the overlap.
The Salt & Sorrow — A sailors' haunt where the house drink is named for a ship that never came back — and one patron swears he was aboard.
The Brass Lantern — Lit at all hours; the owner buys secrets by the candle and the price drops as the wick burns down.
The Cloven Hoof — A roadhouse with a back room where a goat-masked broker sets prices on jobs no one will say aloud.
The Drowned Crown — Built over a flooded throne room; the cellar floods at high tide and the regulars bet on what surfaces.
The Last Lamp — The final inn before the moor road. The keeper rents lanterns and never asks why travelers don't bring them back.
The Wandering Stoat — A tavern that quietly moves one street over every season; locals shrug, newcomers panic.
The Cracked Tankard — Cheap ale, honest fights, and a barkeep who keeps a tally of every grudge sworn under his roof.
The Hanged Man's Rest — Named for the gallows it replaced. The cheapest room is the one directly over the old trapdoor.
The Velvet Antler — An upscale lodge for hunters; the trophies on the wall include at least one thing that shouldn't exist.
The Mended Sail — A harbor inn run by a retired smuggler who still knows which tide carries which cargo.
The Ember & Oak — Warm, woodsmoke, good stew — and a hearth that hasn't gone out in ninety years, by someone's design.
The Toll Witch — A crossroads tavern where the old woman at the door collects a 'toll' that isn't always money.
The Copper Kettle — Famous for a soup recipe the cook guards with a contract signed in something darker than ink.
The Silent Fiddle — A bard plays here nightly without making a sound; patrons hear the music only after they leave.
The Three Crows — Three carved crows over the door. Locals say when a fourth appears, someone in the room won't see morning.
The Rusty Anchor — Landlocked, a hundred miles from any sea, with a genuine ship's anchor no one can explain.
The Frostbitten Fox — A mountain-pass inn that only opens in winter; in summer the building simply isn't there.
The Honeyed Word — A negotiators' tavern where every booth is warded against eavesdropping — for a steep hourly rate.
The Boar's Tooth — Mercenary hangout; the job board out front is older than the building and never goes empty.
The Weeping Widow — The portrait above the bar weeps real tears on the anniversary of a murder no one will name.
The Painted Veil — A masquerade is held nightly; nobody removes their mask, and the staff prefer it that way.
The Stumbling Giant — Built to giant scale from salvaged ruins; the stools require a ladder and the regulars don't mind.
The Quiet Coin — A gambling den disguised as a sleepy inn. The house always wins, and the house is not the owner.
The Iron Maidenhead — A smith-turned-keeper serves ale in repurposed helmets and won't say who wore them.
The Lurid Lily — A flower that blooms only at midnight grows in the courtyard; its pollen loosens tongues.
The Broken Wheel — A caravan stop where a wainwright fixes wagons and, for the right price, arranges for them to break.
The Moth & Flame — Beautiful, doomed, and packed nightly; three inns have burned on this lot and patrons keep coming.
The Pickled Imp — A jar behind the bar holds something small and red that the owner insists is 'just a novelty.'
The Sunken Bell — A drowned chapel bell tolls under the floorboards at odd hours; the keeper charges extra to sleep through it.
The Grinning Skull — A necromancer's old haunt; the skull over the door answers yes-or-no questions for a copper.
The Tilted Spire — Leans more each year. Bets on the night it finally falls are the inn's real business.
The Amber Hart — A genteel coaching inn whose guestbook is a forger's masterpiece — half the names never stayed.
The Crooked Candle — Every candle burns at an angle, pointing, the superstitious say, toward the nearest liar.
The Howling Cellar — Good rooms upstairs; downstairs is sealed, and on full moons the staff turn the music up loud.
The Maiden's Folly — Built by a noblewoman to spite her family; her ghost approves of patrons who tip the staff well.
The Spit & Whistle — A working-class tap where the dartboard hides a peephole into the back room's high-stakes table.
The Verdant Goat — Overgrown with vines that move when no one watches; the keeper waters them with the dregs.
The Black Kettle — A witch runs the kitchen and the rumor mill in equal measure; her stew cures more than hunger.
The Lucky Stump — Built around a stump no axe will cut. Rub it before a wager — most regulars swear by it.
The Whistling Pig — The taxidermied boar over the bar whistles a warning tune whenever the watch is near.
The Sable Door — Members only. There is no sign, no name on the deed, and a very long list of people forbidden entry.
The Foundered Galleon — A whole ship's hull hauled inland and roofed over; the captain's quarters are the priciest suite.
The Twin Daggers — Two knives crossed over the hearth; pull either free and the whole room goes very, very still.
The Mossy Stone — A druid-friendly inn at the forest's edge where the ale is brewed from spring water and old pacts.
The Candlewick Inn — Run by a family of chandlers; each room's candle is keyed to its guest and gutters when they lie.
The Ragged Banner — A war banner hangs in tatters above the bar; veterans drink free, and they always seem to know each other.
The Glass Minnow — A riverside tavern with a tank of silver fish said to swim toward whoever will die first that night.
The Hollow Crown Tap — A deposed king tends bar under a false name; half the patrons know and the other half are spies.
The Wyrm's Repose — Carved into a hillside that locals insist is a sleeping dragon; rent is cheap and nerves are not.

tavernRumors.name: Tavern Rumors & Hooks
items: Old Tam's scarecrow faces a different way every morning, I swear it. — It turns to watch something coming down from the hills. Tam nailed it in place last week; now it screams at dusk.

The baroness hasn't left her tower since the eclipse, they say. — The baroness died years ago. Her maid writes the decrees — fairly, by all accounts. The heir who just learned this is neither fair nor patient.
Ferryman's charging double after dark now. Won't say why. — The far bank isn't the same place after sunset. He charges double because half his night passengers never disembark.

There's a chest of pay-silver buried under the old gallows, I heard. — There isn't. The magistrate planted the tale to catch grave-robbers. Last night's diggers found something anyway, and now they're missing.
The king's new coin won't tarnish, melt, nor bend. Lucky metal, they're saying. — It's not metal. The mint's 'new vein' is a sleeping thing being shaved coin by coin, and it is beginning to notice.

Goodwife Pell's pies win the fair every year, and nobody's ever seen her orchard. — There is no orchard. There's a door in her cellar that's sometimes an orchard. Lately it has been autumn there far too long.
That soldier at the end of the bar buys two ales and drinks one. — The second is for the friend he carried home in his pack. He still carries the pack. Nobody has asked what's in it.

Grain barges go upriver full and come back down full. Strange trade, that. — True. The grain is bought, blessed, and sold back as tithe. The temple sells the kingdom its own harvest twice; the ledger names a duke.

Children over in Harlow keep drawing the same tower. There's no tower in Harlow. — Not yet, there isn't. The drawings grow more detailed weekly. The newest include a door, standing open, and a small crowd walking in.

Wolves took six sheep from the Aldercott fold in one night. Six! — No wolf. The sheep walked out single file, uphill. The shepherd boy counted them going and said nothing, because they told him not to.

Someone stole the mayor's portrait. Just the canvas — frame's still hanging. — The portrait left on its own; it had seen enough. It's been spotted in three taverns, talking. It knows where the levy money went.

Lighthouse keeper's gone mad, they say. Burns the lamp green some nights. — Green is the old distress code. She's sane, besieged, and signaling the only way she can. Someone ashore keeps insisting she's mad.
Don't drink at the Crooked Stile. A man lost a whole week there. — He sold the week to the landlord, to forget something. The landlord resells memories upstairs, and yours would fetch a fine price.

That's the third tax collector gone missing on the King's Road this season. — All three arrived safely at one manor, where a retired general buys soldiers' debts with the taxes. He isn't stealing — he's recruiting.
Our bells toll by themselves whenever somebody's dying. Always have. — They do. Last night they tolled for the mayor, who is in perfect health and suddenly very interested in hiring guards.

New priest won't take confessions anymore. Locks the booth up at night. — Something in the booth keeps confessing — old sins, in the old priest's voice. The new priest checked the grave. A stranger is buried in it.
Road north's closed. Bridge out, the wardens say. — The bridge is fine. The wardens are paid to route travelers past an inn that counts them. Someone is taking a census of armed strangers.

Hangman retired sudden-like. Won't touch rope, won't say why. — His last client thanked him by a birth-name nobody living should know. Now he's buying the sealed trial records, and someone keeps outbidding him.

They found the duke's hunting party safe and well. Horses won't go near them, though. — The horses know. The party that returned has one more rider than rode out, and no two witnesses agree on which face is new.
That cat's not left its stool in a fortnight. Hisses if you shift it. — The cat is a wizard who lost his body in a wager. The winner wears it in here every Thursday, and the cat counts Thursdays.

Orphanage has a new benefactor. Anonymous, and pays in old gold. — The coins predate the kingdom. The founder has woken, found her orphanage still standing four centuries on, and resumed payments. She visits at midwinter.

The witch up Hag's Hollow is cursing cattle. Milk's come red twice this month. — The 'witch' is a midwife who knows whose child the reeve fathered. The reeve dyes the milk himself, building the village toward a burning.

Stonecutter's gone stone deaf, and he's never looked happier. Queer old soul. — The quarry's new seam speaks to anyone who can hear it. He deafened himself with his own chisels. The next shift starts at dawn.

Peace with the hill clans by autumn! A herald said so in this very room. — The herald's livery is real; the peace isn't. The true herald, three days behind, carries a declaration of war. Someone profits from three calm days.

Fisherfolk are pulling up coins instead of cod off the point. Whole nets full. — True. A sunken town is emptying its treasury upward, buying the surface's silence before something deeper evicts them too. The refugees arrive next tide.

Old Cobb proposes to Widow Hale every market day. She always laughs him off. — They've been secretly wed thirty years; the proposal is a signal meaning all is well. Last market he didn't ask, and only she noticed.

They've doubled the guard on the granary. Rats, they're saying. Big ones. — Not rats. Child-sized footprints lead in but never out, and the grain count rises nightly. Whatever lives there is paying rent in wheat.

There's a duelist at the crossroads inn challenges every blade passing through. Never loses. — He's cursed to duel until honestly beaten. He bribes opponents to train harder, desperate to lose. His gold is running out; his restraint too.

The alchemist's tower exploded Tuesday. He's fine. Smiling, even. Suspicious, that. — The explosion was the experiment succeeding. He's twenty years younger and dodging creditors who can't prove the old man's debts are legally his.

Don't shortcut through Wether's Field. Folk come out the other side weeping. — The field replays your worst goodbye, once each. The old lord pays something nightly for repeat performances, and the price now walks behind him.

Bandits in the Speltwood took a whole wedding party last week. Rings and all. — The bandit chief returns everything within days, with interest. He's laundering a dead lord's hoard back into the valley. Stopping him beggars three villages.
Mountain pass opened a month early this year. Lucky for trade, eh? — Something cleared it. The first caravan through reported the snow banked neatly, as if shoveled. The second caravan is overdue.

Schoolmaster's teaching the children their letters in some foreign script now. Fancy ideas. — The script is dead and binding. Read together, the children's copybooks form a contract. Find the other signatory before term ends.
They say the queen's food taster has outlived three queens. — True — he ate the poison every time and lived. Now dying, he's auctioning the names behind each dose. Bidding opens tonight, upstairs.

That beggar by the south gate gives coin away some days. Mad, surely. — He pays folk to stand exactly where he says. He's arranging the town into a pattern, person by person, and it's nearly complete.
The lord's son is back from the war. Won't even see his own mother. — His shadow didn't come back with him. It's walking home overland; he tracks its progress on a map. He no longer thinks it's his.

Stable boy at the Black Ram talks to horses. Worse — they wait their turn. — The horses elected him their voice. Their first formal grievance concerns the knackerman's side-trade, and they have evidence.

Quarantine flag's up over Millbrook, but nobody's sick. My cousin swears it. — True, nobody's sick. The flag keeps help away while the village starves out something that arrived in a grain cart and now holds the church.

Glassblower's made nothing but eyes for a month. Crates and crates of them. — They're commissioned. Every statue in the capital receives new eyes before coronation day. Someone intends to watch the crowds through them.

Midwife says not one babe's been born in the valley since midwinter. — They're born elsewhere. Mothers wake delivered, healthy, alone, with a paid receipt nailed to the door. Nobody has yet tried to redeem one.

Council's taken to meeting at midnight now. For the quiet, they claim. — Midnight is when the petitioner arrives — something drowned-voiced, with lawful claims older than the town charter. The council is losing the negotiation politely.

Them brothers fenced their farm clean down the middle. Split the well, even. — The fence isn't spite. Something is buried lengthwise beneath it, and each brother believes the other volunteered to keep watch. Neither did.
Royal astronomer got sacked. Drunkenness, the palace says. — He's sober. He found a star that is getting closer and refused to call it a comet. His charts were seized; one copy wasn't.

Brewster's new ale tastes different to every man who drinks it. Same cask! — Each cup tastes of the drinker's childhood home; refugees pay anything. Her wellspring wasn't under the floor last year, and somewhere, something misses it.

Gravedigger's been measuring folk with his eyes lately. Gives me chills. — He was paid for twelve graves in advance, names sealed in an envelope he's forbidden to open. The thirteenth he dug free, for himself.

More pilgrims through today, asking after a shrine nobody here has heard of. — The shrine is real; the village stands inside it, unknowing. Pilgrims see what residents can't, and they've begun kneeling to the cooper's daughter.

They've banned dice at the Gilded Goose. Even the dominoes are gone. — One gambler couldn't lose for three nights and wept the whole time. The luck is stolen property, and its owner is coming to collect.

King's stonemasons were surveying our little chapel yesterday. Ours! Imagine. — True. The chapel's cornerstone is the kingdom's lost charter-stone — crown law flows from wherever it sits. Three parties have just realized that.

npcQuirks.name: NPC Quirks & Mannerisms
items: Counts everything twice — Coins, stairs, people in the room. A merchant once shorted them everything they had; being certain is the scar.
Never says goodbye — Just leaves. The last person they said it to didn't come back, and they've decided the word is the problem.
Addresses everyone by profession — 'Baker. Soldier. Thief.' Claims names are for friends, and they're rationing those.
Always sits facing the door — And will pay, charm, or intimidate to get that chair. Knows exactly who might walk in someday.
Apologizes to objects — Bumped tables, dropped tools, a kicked stone. Grew up around a hedge-witch who insisted everything keeps score.
Tastes a pinch of salt before business — Old superstition: salt breaks glamours. Twice in their life, it has.
Quotes a dead philosopher constantly — Half the quotes are invented. The philosopher is invented too, which a literate party member might eventually notice.
Keeps shaking hands a beat too long — They're counting your pulse. A healer by training, they can't stop checking whether people are well — or lying.
Whistles the same four notes — It's the first half of a signal from their smuggling years. They've never heard anyone whistle the second half. If someone does, everything changes.
Refuses to be drawn or described — Turns from sketch artists, deflects questions about their face. Somewhere, a portrait is hunting for its subject.
Feeds every animal they meet — Crusts in every pocket. They believe one of the strays in this city is a transformed prince, and they intend to be remembered kindly.
Never touches money directly — Gloves, cloth, a coin-tray. They once held a cursed sovereign for an afternoon and the month that followed is why they flinch.
Corrects everyone's grammar mid-crisis — Pedantry is how they keep their hands from shaking. The worse the danger, the more precise they get.
Collects buttons from the dead — One per funeral, with the family's blessing — usually. A jar of them sits on their shelf, and they can name every one.
Asks permission before entering any room — Loudly, of the room itself. They lived a year in a house that punished anyone who didn't.
Always eats dessert first — A soldier's habit: never die before the best part. The campaigns are over; the philosophy stayed.

Lies about small things only — The weather, what they had for lunch, the color of a passing cat. Big things they tell with unsettling honesty. The small lies are practice for one large one they're saving.
Stacks anything stackable — Coins, crates, polite arguments. Disorder physically pains them; an enemy who scatters a stack mid-negotiation learns what their anger looks like.
Hums when someone lies — Doesn't know they do it. Everyone else in the room learns the tell within a week, which makes them the most dangerous dinner guest in the city.
Wears a single glove — Switches hands daily. The bare hand is for friends; the gloved one signed something they regret.
Names their weapons after exes — Cheerfully introduces each one. The newest knife has no name yet, and they're seeing someone.
Tips outrageously, tracks it precisely — A ledger of every gratuity ever given. They're buying the city's goodwill one coin at a time and intend to collect, all at once, on one specific day.
Speaks to their shadow when thinking — 'What do we reckon?' The shadow has never answered. They keep asking because once — just once — it nodded.
Refuses all chairs but stools — Backs of chairs block escape routes. Ask them where they learned that and watch the friendly conversation end.
Memorizes exits aloud — 'Door, window, cellar hatch.' A fire took their first shop and the habit is the memorial.
Polishes one specific coin — Not currency — entry fee. They've been told a door will one day ask for it, and the teller has been right about everything else so far.
Bows to thresholds — A small nod at every doorway. Their grandmother swore doorways are where the dead wait, and rudeness is remembered.
Eats only food someone else has tasted — Frames it as etiquette, performs it like ritual. Three poisonings in one family teach table manners no court ever could.
Laughs at exactly the wrong moments — Funerals, sentencings, confessions. The laugh is a curse — literally; the witch who cast it said only one thing un-says it.
Gives directions by taverns — 'Left at the Salt & Sorrow, straight past the Gilded Eel.' Has never learned a street name; has never once been lost.
Keeps checking a watch that doesn't run — Stopped at a quarter to four, years ago. They look anyway — not to know the time, but to remember what happened at it.
Introduces themselves with a different title each time — Captain, Doctor, Curator, Widow. All technically true, each from a life they finished and folded away like laundry.
Won't step on shadows of people — Weaves oddly down crowded streets. Where they're from, stepping on a shadow is an assault, and the constables there agree.
Saves the last sip of every drink — Pours it out at the door for 'whoever's listening.' Once, the night after they forgot, was the worst night of their life.
Asks everyone's mother's name — Files them away, uses them with surgical effect — 'Would Marta approve of this?' Negotiators hate them. Mothers adore them.
Carries chalk everywhere — Marks small symbols on walls they pass: safe, unsafe, listening. The marks are in thieves' cant, and the thieves want to know who's been grading their city.
Repeats your last word back as a question — 'Question?' It buys them three seconds to think, which is how they've won every bargain in living memory.
Never sits with their back to water — Rivers, harbors, even a full bath. Something in the water knows their face, and they extend it no opportunities.
Compulsively trues crooked things — Pictures, ledgers, hat brims. The day everything in their shop hung straight on its own is the day they stopped sleeping there.

Mourns aloud for strangers — Reads the public death notices each morning and grieves each one for exactly a minute. Someone has to, they say. Lately the notices have started including a name not yet dead.
Refuses to whistle indoors — And goes quietly pale when others do. In their sailing years, whistling indoors called the wind — and the wind, once, answered inside the hull.
Always pays in exact change — To the copper, counted into your palm. They once owed a debt that grew at terrifying interest, and round numbers feel like the start of another one.

Talks about themselves in the plural — 'We think,' 'we'd rather not.' Possibly royalty in exile, possibly a twin who didn't survive, possibly — listen closely on quiet nights — exactly what it sounds like.
Sniffs all paper before reading it — A scribe's habit from the censor's office: certain inks lie, and certain letters bite. They've caught two of the second kind.
Keeps an empty chair at every meal — Sets a place, pours a cup, lets it cool untouched. The expected guest has been late for eleven years; the standard isn't dropping now.
Recites prices from memory, eyes closed — Every transaction of their career, retrievable. Close their eyes mid-haggle and the market goes quiet — the Ledger is consulting itself.
Wears mourning gray one day a week — Always the same weekday, never an explanation. The city has invented eleven theories. The truth is worse than nine of them.
Tests every rope, rail, and rung twice — A rigger's discipline from the fleet. The one time they didn't is the reason for the limp, and the limp is the reason they test.
Calls everyone by the wrong name — consistently — You'll be 'Henrik' forever; correction is futile. The names aren't random: they're casting a play, one citizen at a time, and opening night is real.

Leaves every gathering exactly at the bell — Mid-sentence, mid-deal, mid-dance. A standing appointment they've kept nightly for years — and no one who's followed them has ever seen them arrive anywhere.

cityTownNames.name: City & Town Names
items: Vessmark — A river city built on grain barges chained together; each autumn the chains are cut and re-drawn — and so are the old debts.
Cinderhollow — A mining town whose deep shafts went quiet years ago, but the lift cages still come up on schedule — scrubbed clean.
Bellwether — Famous for a bronze bell that rings itself before disasters. It rang twice this morning.
Saltreach — A port where the tide retreats a full mile at dusk, baring a drowned older town the locals refuse to map.
Thornhaven — The living hedge-wall that protected the town for a century has begun growing inward.
Greywater Crossing — A toll-bridge town where the toll is never coin — the keeper asks every traveler for one true secret.
Emberlyn — The lantern-makers' city. The night its lights go out, every guild contract in the realm is void — so someone guards the flame, and someone else studies it.
Hollowmere — The lake at its center has never returned a dropped rope, a sounding stone, or the one rowboat that's always missing.
Kingsfall — Named for the king who died here. His heirs keep paying handsomely for the silence of anyone who asks exactly how.
Marrowgate — The city gate is carved from a single colossal bone, and scholars pay in gold to learn what creature it came from.
Dunrowan — A hill town that elects its mayor by whichever candidate survives a winter alone in the watchtower. This year, both did.
Pellgrim's Rest — A pilgrim road town with more inns than houses — and a shrine whose relic was quietly replaced with a fake nobody dares expose.
Coppervein — The mines never produced copper — the name covers what they actually bring up, which the crown taxes as 'copper' with a wink.
Mistral Reach — A cliff city of wind-mills and signal flags where the law arrives by carrier hawk and leaves by rumor.
Oxbridge — Grew rich charging armies to cross its only ford; both sides of the current war are somehow on the ledger.
Faldenwood — A logging town that cuts only fallen trees. Lately, more trees fall in the night than any storm explains.
Harrowfield — Its famous black soil yields three harvests a year — and one night a year, the fields harvest back.
Brindlemarch — A border town with two names, two flags, and two tax collectors; the locals long ago stopped telling either kingdom the truth.
Gloamport — Ships only dock here at twilight — the harbor rocks shift at noon and midnight, and the pilot guild keeps the timetable secret.
Stonewake — Built in the wake of a petrified giant; the masons swear the stone is warmer every spring.
Larkspur — A garden town whose flowers are exported as dyes, perfumes, and — according to three dead alchemists — something else.
Redgate — The gate was painted with the blood of an oathbreaker king, and it weeps in wet weather. Tourists love it. The priests don't.
Ashvale — Rebuilt seven times on its own ashes; the eighth town charter forbids asking why anyone stays.
Quillhollow — A scribes' town that copies books for every court in the land — including, for the right price, copies that differ by one crucial line.
Tarnwick — The candle-makers here render a wax that burns underwater. The navy wants the recipe; the widows who make it want the navy gone.
Hearthstead — Every house shares one great chimney-spirit that demands a story each solstice — and remembers every lie it's told.
Galewatch — A storm-warning town on the headland; its lighthouse keepers are all deaf, and all claim the wind tells them things anyway.
Mournbrook — The brook runs clear except on execution days in the capital, three hundred miles away, when it runs dark.
Silverstrand — A beach town that pans silver dust from the surf each new moon — and posts armed wardens to keep anyone from following the dust out to sea.
Crowsperch — The rookery above town is older than the town. The crows hold grudges, keep treasures, and occasionally pay for favors.
Fenwick Hollow — A marsh town on stilts where the houses are re-measured every spring — because the hollow is slowly, patiently sinking on one side.
Goldenfall — Named for autumn leaves, not treasure, which doesn't stop one doomed expedition a year from digging up the orchards.
Ironmoor — The moor's bog iron makes the finest blades in the region — and the smiths' guild quietly buries every sword that comes back from the moor already rusted.
Vantage — A garrison town on the only pass through the mountains; its commander hasn't received orders in nine years and has stopped admitting it.
Willowmere — The healing springs draw nobles from three kingdoms — all of whom pretend not to see each other, which makes it the best listening post in the realm.
Duskhaven — A sanctuary city where any fugitive may claim one year of protection; the trick is surviving the other fugitives.
Cobblestone Cross — Four trade roads, one square, and a centuries-old rule: no weapon may be drawn within sight of the crossroads stone. The stone has been missing since Tuesday.
Palewater — The river runs milk-white from the glacier caves; those who drink it dream true once — and never again.
Rooksend — The last town before the wastes, where every expedition buys its supplies, hires its guides, and writes its will at the same counter.
Amberhold — The keep's walls are veined with amber that preserves whatever touches it; the duke's gallery of 'statues' grows by one or two a decade.
Threadneedle — A weavers' city whose tapestries are bought by every court — partly for the artistry, partly because unpicking them reveals next season's politics.
Stormbreak — The harbor's breakwater is a sleeping leviathan's spine — maintained, fed, and above all never discussed during storm season.
Wyrmditch — The 'ditch' is a claw-furrow a mile long; the town festival celebrates the dragon that made it, on the theory that flattery has worked so far.
Lanternlea — Meadow town where will-o'-wisps are licensed, leashed, and rented out as night-guides — mostly trustworthy, always listening.
Karst — Built over a honeycomb of sinkholes; property here is sold by depth, and the cheapest deeds come with a rope ladder.
Olliven — An olive-press town whose first pressing belongs, by ancient pact, to a god nobody worships anymore — and the one year they skipped it, so did spring.
Bittermarsh — Its peat preserves everything: bog-bodies, lost banners, and grudges. The peat-cutters' union doubles as the town's historians and blackmailers.
Highcairn — Every traveler adds a stone to the great cairn at the summit gate; removing one is the only crime the town still hangs for, and no one will say why.
Ferrow — The ferry town's boats are rowed by a hereditary line of silent ferrymen who are paid in copper — and tipped, by the wise, in memories.
Summerhollow — Frost never touches the hollow, even in deep winter — which is lovely for the orchards and increasingly hard to explain to the tax assessor measuring everyone else's dead fields.

factionsGuilds.name: Fantasy Factions & Guild Names
items: The Opened Hand — Motto: "Freely given, freely owed." — A thieves' guild with a reputation for scrupulous honor among members and absolutely no scruple toward outsiders. They donate publicly, steal privately, and keep perfect ledgers of both.

The Iron Compact — Motto: "Terms define us." — A mercenary consortium that enforces contracts with terrifying thoroughness. They've sued nobility in crown court and won. The contract is sacred; the man who signed it, considerably less so.

The Cinder Court — Motto: "What burns, endures." — An arsonist's guild that frames itself as a selective demolition service. Cities hire them to clear slums. Rivals hire them for other reasons. They accept both commissions without moral distinction.

The Gilded Tongue Society — Motto: "A true thing said beautifully is half a lie." — A broker's guild of fixers, diplomats, and translators. Every member is fluent in at least four languages and skilled at making one truth sound like another.

The Order of the Patient Wound — Motto: "We do not forget. We simply wait." — A vengeance-broker organization. Clients pay a retainer; the Order fulfills grievances on its own schedule, sometimes years later. Patience is the product.

The Stewards of the Locked Gate — Motto: "Nothing passes that we have not counted." — A customs and tariff guild that controls three major trade choke-points. Their ledgers are perfect. Their cut is non-negotiable. They call it governance.

Brightwater Cartel — Motto: "Clean money spends best." — A merchant house that runs legitimate river trade on top and a smuggling network underneath. They genuinely believe the two operations are separate.

The Unbroken Circle — Motto: "What is shared cannot be stolen." — A communal arcane order that pools spellbook knowledge and splits spell-slot debt across the membership. Outsiders find this philosophy baffling. Members find it efficient.

The Shrouded Cartographers — Motto: "The map you don't have is worth more than the one you do." — A secret society of surveyors who deliberately leave certain regions off official maps. They sell accurate versions to a very short list of clients.

The Brass Brotherhood — Motto: "Every wheel must turn." — A guild of engineers, tinkerers, and clock-makers that controls the city's water distribution. They negotiate from a position of infrastructure.

The Night Registrar — Motto: "All debts are written. All writing endures." — A loan-shark guild that records every debt in magical ink that cannot be destroyed. Their scribes attend executions to write off bad accounts in person.

The Woven Veil — Motto: "We see the cloth, not the thread." — An intelligence network disguised as a textile merchants' association. Their couriers move coded messages in bolt-end stamps. No one who matters thinks spies read fabric.

The Sevenfold Assembly — Motto: "No one speaks for all of us." — A decentralized criminal collective where each cell knows only one other. Dismantling them is like cutting fog. They have no leader by design and no loyalty beyond the cell.

The Red Ledger — Motto: "The account must balance." — An assassins' guild that frames itself as an arbitration service. Disputes that can't be resolved at the table go to the Red Ledger's second, bloodier department.

The Fellowship of the Open Road — Motto: "The road takes and the road gives." — A caravan-guard and bandit hybrid: they protect caravans from bandits who are, in many cases, also them. They call the premium a 'road tax' and the paperwork is genuinely excellent.

The Collegium of Pale Fires — Motto: "Knowledge illuminates what wisdom cannot." — A necromantic research order that operates out of three cities simultaneously under different names. Their founding charter predates the laws against them.

The Copper Syndicate — Motto: "Small coins, everywhere." — A widespread network of petty criminals, pickpockets, and information sellers. No individual job is large. The aggregate is staggering. Their monthly revenue rivals minor nobility.

The Vigilant Candle — Motto: "Darkness is not the enemy — complacency is." — A monster-hunting order with genuine civic purpose and deeply complicated finances. Half their funding comes from the monsters they create demand to fight.

House Kethravane — Motto: "Blood remembers." — A merchant noble house that has survived four regime changes by having a daughter in every succession. They collect genealogies the way others collect treasure, and use them the same way.

The Ironthroat Company — Motto: "We keep what we kill." — A mercenary band with a strict no-survivors policy on the other side and an equally strict profit-sharing policy on their own. Veterans stay for decades. The work is grim but the pension is real.

The Quiet Consistory — Motto: "Let the work speak." — A secret magical research group that publishes results anonymously and purges their own names from the record. They genuinely don't want credit. The reason for that varies by member.

The Dock Levy — Motto: "Everything that floats pays." — A waterfront protection guild so embedded in port operations that the harbormaster's office has been meaningless for thirty years. Newcomers discover this on their first invoice.

The Restored Order of Dust — Motto: "We have seen empires end." — An ancient monastic order that collects ruins, lost texts, and dying languages. They are not interested in power; they are interested in recording power's inevitable failure. This makes them very popular with the powerful, who can't quite explain why.

The Embered Crown — Motto: "The throne is a promise, not a seat." — A legitimist faction loyal to a monarchy dissolved two generations ago. They maintain a succession claim, a pretender (currently twelve years old), and a great deal of patience.

The Silkhand Collective — Motto: "Touch nothing you do not mean to own." — A fence network specializing in magical and antique items. They authenticate everything, value nothing sentimentally, and charge accordingly. Their appraisers have better taste than most museums.

The Brotherhood of the Necessary Wound — Motto: "The physician cuts to save." — A religious militant order that frames political assassination as a form of surgery. Their theology is internally consistent and their targets are very, very specific.

The Harrowgate Compact — Motto: "The law is a road. We maintain it." — A guild of bounty hunters and writs-servers that technically operates inside the law. Their reading of 'technically' is aggressive and has been tested several times in court. They keep winning.

The Secondlight Institute — Motto: "Every flame has a shadow." — A school of divinatory magic that sells futures to wealthy clients. Their forecasts are accurate enough to be valuable and vague enough to survive being wrong. The business model is ancient.

The Verdant Chain — Motto: "Root and branch endure the storm." — A druidic faction with commercial interests in forest and farmland. They oppose logging, mine development, and road-building with a combination of protest, sabotage, and property law. All three tools get used.

The Long Sorrow Guild — Motto: "Grief is a profession." — A guild of professional mourners, obituarists, and estate-clearers. They attend every funeral in three cities, hear everything, and write down what matters. Their archive is the city's real history.

The Sable Covenant — Motto: "An oath is its own prison." — A secret society that binds members with magical oaths at initiation. The exact terms of those oaths are not explained beforehand. Most members find them reasonable. Most.

The Forgeborn Alliance — Motto: "What is made well, lasts." — A master-smiths' guild that refuses to compete on price. Their work is expensive, contractually guaranteed, and carries a maker's mark that has functioned as a kind of currency for a century.

The Twice-Sworn Guard — Motto: "Loyalty, then law." — A bodyguard company whose members swear first to the client, then to the Crown. The order of precedence has mattered, historically. They are expensive specifically because of this clause.

The Pale Standard — Motto: "We carry the line where others break." — A disciplined mercenary infantry company known for holding retreating positions while clients escape. They charge for this service in advance. They have never needed to offer a refund.

The Oathbound Conclave — Motto: "We are the law we swore." — A paladin-led organization that operates as judge, jury, and sometimes executioner in regions without functioning courts. They are scrupulously fair by their own standards, and occasionally terrifying.

The Glass Registry — Motto: "All things are transparent to those who look." — An information-brokering guild that publishes nothing and sells everything. Their office has no sign. Clients find it by being sent there by someone who was helped.

The Saltborn League — Motto: "The sea takes impartially; so do we." — A privateer confederation that operates under letters of marque from three different sovereigns simultaneously. Their legal status depends entirely on which port they're in.

The Greymantle Society — Motto: "Neutral ground has a price." — An organization that sells venue and mediation for negotiations between factions at war. Their locations are inviolable by tradition and self-interest. They have ejected armed parties from four faction wars and been proven right each time.

The Root & Remedy — Motto: "A sick city is a cheap city." — An apothecaries' guild that controls medicinal herb supply across six districts. They heal generously and price gouge on the rarer cures. The poor get the former; the wealthy get the bill.

The Stonewright Clan — Motto: "We built what you stand on." — A stonecutters' and architects' guild that has quietly placed a binding easement on nearly every civic building in the city. Renovations, alterations, or demolitions all require their sign-off. This is technically legal.

The Amber Court — Motto: "We preserve what others discard." — A collector's society that acquires cursed objects, forbidden texts, and politically inconvenient artifacts and stores them. They are entirely serious about the storage part. The question is what happens when the bill comes due.

The Reaper's Ledge — Motto: "All bets settled in full." — A gambling syndicate that runs games in three tiers: public houses for common play, private salons for merchants, and a third level the organization denies exists. Debts from the third tier are collected differently.

The Unmarked Congregation — Motto: "Faith does not require a face." — A mystery cult with no public iconography, no named gods, and no traceable clergy. Members wear no symbols. They are identified in public only by what they don't do: swear oaths, enter temples, or eat certain foods.

The Last Commission — Motto: "Every great work was someone's last." — A guild of aging master craftspeople who take on only final, definitive projects: the bridge that will stand forever, the vault door that will never be opened, the monument that will outlast the nation that ordered it.

The Whistler's Union — Motto: "Sound carries farther than the spoken word." — A courier network that communicates via coded birdsong, flute calls, and street vendor cries. Their message system predates the post. Cities that have tried to shut them down find they need them within six months.

House Varenthis — Motto: "Old roots drink deep." — A noble house in managed decline that has converted its fading political power into financial expertise. They hold debts on half the ambitious families in the city and collect interest in political favors, not coin.

The Tallow Brotherhood — Motto: "We light the way for those who pay." — A chandlers' guild that has parlayed control of city lighting contracts into a remarkable intelligence network. Every lamplighter is a trained observer. The Brotherhood sees the city better than the watch does.

The Crimson Attestation — Motto: "Blood is the only signature that cannot be forged." — A blood-magic notary guild whose contracts are binding in ways no conventional law can override. Their services are legal in four jurisdictions, illegal in nine, and desperately sought in all of them.

The Wandering Moot — Motto: "Jurisdiction ends at the city wall." — A traveling court of arbiters who rule on disputes between parties with no common nationality, no shared law, and no neutral ground. They convene wherever needed, decide by precedent, and have accumulated three hundred years of case law that no single government recognizes but everyone uses.

dungeonRooms.name: Random Dungeon Rooms
items: An armory, fully stocked, every blade oiled and gleaming. — The garrison fled and took nothing. Whatever came, they decided weapons wouldn't help — and the racks have been restocked since.
A cavern ceiling furred with ten thousand bats — awake, silent, not leaving. — Their exit is blocked. Something new sits in their doorway, and the whole colony is waiting for it to finish eating.
Forty sarcophagi, every lid slid open, every one empty. — Not robbed — out. Once a year the dead walk home to visit the living. They return by dawn, and they count the beds.

Stairs descend into clear floodwater, lit faintly from somewhere below. — The light is a lantern on a drowned surveyor's belt. He's still down there, still walking, still mapping — and his map is nearly finished.

A sewer junction of four tunnels; one is bricked shut from the inside. — Fresh mortar, scratched with names: the masons sealed themselves in with what they caught. Some of the names are still being added.

A round chamber: furniture bolted to the floor, one door set in the ceiling. — Gravity flips on the hour. Everything loose — including the wizard's keyring glinting on the ceiling — takes turns falling.

Six armed bandits who instantly drop their weapons and surrender. — They surrender to everyone; it's how they get escorted past the thing on level three. They're polite, helpful, and lying about the treasure room.
Under a glass dome on a pedestal: one plain iron key. — It opens every lock below — including the doors built to keep things in. The dome isn't security. It muffles the scratching.

Brass birds on perches, dozens, every tiny head tracking the door. — Clockwork spies that sing their reports when wound. Their master died years ago; decades of dungeon intelligence waits in their songs.
A child-sized tomb, deep underground, with fresh flowers. — The mother brings them daily. She's a ghoul now and has never eaten from this grave. She begs you to end her before hunger wins.
Gnolls in clean surcoats playing dice beneath a framed treaty. — The treaty grants them this level for keeping one door shut. They're behind on the terms and will quietly sell the door's location.

Hundreds of rats sitting upright, silent, all facing the same wall. — The wall sweats something nourishing once a day and feeds them. It's late today, and the rats have begun glancing at the visitors.

A dragon's hoard, every coin copper, stacked in immaculate towers. — The dragon is young, small, and desperately proud. Mock the hoard and earn a century-long enemy; appraise it kindly and earn something rarer.

A banquet for thirty, every dish carved from marble — bread, boar, wine. — Not carved: petrified mid-toast. The thirtieth chair is empty, and the guest of honor they were toasting is still somewhere in the dungeon.

A library where every spine reads the same: 'DO NOT READ THIS.' — Opening any book copies one of your memories into it. The shelves hold three centuries of stolen afternoons, and the librarian buys and sells.

An embalming room, tools laid out, one table occupied beneath a sheet. — Under the sheet: a wax effigy of one of you, half-finished. The embalmer takes commissions, and someone has already paid the deposit.

A polished lever labeled 'DO NOT PULL,' worn smooth by countless hands. — It rings a bell in the lair below. Not a warning — an etiquette test. Guests who announce themselves get parley; sneaks get the traps.

An abandoned mine face: pickaxes dropped before a fat, glittering gold vein. — Dwarves don't abandon gold. Tap the vein and it taps back, eager. Something down here farms miners, and the bait regrows.
A locked cell holding a tidy old man who greets you by name. — The dungeon's architect, jailed so he could never sell its secrets. He'll map every trap — if you swear to leave him safely locked in.
A massive vault door fitted with a small, dog-sized flap. — The builder couldn't lock his dog out. What guards the vault was once that dog; it still answers to 'good boy,' and still wants out.

A cozy bedroom with daylight streaming through its window — far underground. — The window shows your hometown, live. In one house, someone you know is carefully packing your belongings into a crate marked 'deceased.'

A waist-high mushroom forest; the caps glow whenever anyone speaks. — The spores carry sound. Everything said here replays hours later in the deep caves — including whatever the party just planned aloud.
A troll asleep under a sewer bridge, hugging a sign: 'ON STRIKE.' — The dungeon's monsters have unionized. He'll wave anyone through who agrees to deliver their demands to the management below.

A fountain brimming with coins; the basin reads 'Take what you are owed.' — It pays out honestly — and tallies honestly. Some hands come away rich. Some come away empty. One of yours may come away owing.

A room barricaded from inside; defenders' skeletons huddle around a cold fire. — The journal's last line: 'It imitates rescue.' Down the corridor, a voice is calling for help — and each of you recognizes it differently.

Shelved bell jars, each holding tiny weather: a storm, a snowfall, fog. — The labels are names, not contents. These are prisoners. The fog remembers being a magistrate and will testify against the wizard who bottled him.
A wall of funeral niches; one urn among hundreds is warm. — She refused to disperse before confessing — or being confessed to. Carry her to her murderer's tomb upstairs and she'll name the way out.
An ancient latrine, spotless, with fresh flowers in a little vase. — The dungeon's most feared resident keeps it immaculate. The flowers are a memorial to the last visitor who left a mess.
A freestanding door in the room's center, hinged to nothing. — It opens onto wherever the opener most needs to be — not wants. The last user's footprints stop dead at the threshold, mid-stride.

A steaming hot-spring pool, worn soap, towels still damp. — The dungeon factions share the baths under strict truce. The ogre soaking here will trade strategy gossip with anyone willing to scrub his back.
Murals of heroes clearing this dungeon, room by room — including this room. — The final panel is wet paint: you, here, now. The next panel is blank, and someone has left a loaded brush.

A drowned chapel; kneeling skeletons sway in rows before a stone pulpit. — Not swaying — worshipping. The sermon never ended, and the font holds the only air. Joining the congregation buys passage; interrupting it doesn't.

A small schoolroom: tiny benches, slates, a half-finished alphabet on the board. — Goblin children hide in the cubbies. The 'infestation' the village paid you to clear has been teaching itself to write 'please.'

A vault heaped with treasure, posted with a sign: 'Inventory in progress.' — A devil is auditing the dungeon. Theft doesn't bother him — everything taken simply goes on the owner's bill, at interest, with your names as witnesses.

A collapsed stairwell spanned by a new rope ladder and a coin jar. — An enterprising kobold charges toll and sells trap insurance. His prices are fair, his intelligence is better, and the floor below hates him personally.
This room is an exact copy of the last one — including your footprints. — The dungeon duplicates rooms when it's nervous. The copies get sloppier the closer you walk toward whatever it's hiding.

A plague pit, lime-dusted and decades sealed, marker worn smooth. — One name on the marker is chiseled fresh this week. The man it names is alive upstairs — and paying the dungeon's priest for early burial.

A glass-still underground lake; on its island, a single worn chair. — Sit, and the lake replays the death of anything drowned in it — including a murder the local lord pays the boatman to keep underwater.

A chalk summoning circle, badly smudged, currently occupied by a calm cow. — The swap went both ways: somewhere a demon stands baffled in a pasture. The cow knows the return-word and has no reason to say it.
A corridor of traps, each politely labeled: 'PIT.' 'DARTS.' 'FLAME.' — The labels are accurate and the traps disarmed. This is a training hall, and the graduating class's final exam just walked in.

A looted royal tomb; the skeleton inside wears a fresh paper crown. — The real crown sits on a usurper upstairs. The paper one is renewed yearly — treason by craft — and the palace pays dearly for the artist's name.
A greased waterwheel turning in the sewer flow, geared into the wall. — It winds something enormous one tooth per day. The maintenance log beside it is meticulous, and it ends next week.
A minotaur hunched over a chalk map of his own labyrinth, frowning. — He's lost and too proud to admit it. He'll trade the maze's true path if you let him pretend he rescued you.
Every sound here arrives twice — and the echo comes half a second early. — The room remembers forward. Right now it's echoing a scream that nobody in the party has screamed yet.

A hermit monk copying a book by candlelight; the same page, sixty years. — The book is the dungeon's deed and wipes itself each dawn. Whoever finishes copying it owns everything below — and everything below knows he's close.

A scale model of the dungeon on a table, exquisite down to the dust. — Move a piece and the dungeon moves. The previous owner is sealed in a wall somewhere because someone nudged his miniature — which is also here.
Through a crack in the cave wall: wind, smelling of rain and grass. — There is no surface there. Something deep learned that prisoners dig fastest toward hope, and it needs this tunnel finished.

A suggestion box bolted beside an ironbound door, quills and paper provided. — Management reads every note and renovates accordingly. Good ideas are paid in keys. Last month, somebody suggested 'more skeletons.'

questHooks.name: Quest Hooks
items: The Tax That Eats — A village pays a 'grain tithe' to a shrine in the hills. The grain keeps something asleep, and this year's harvest failed.
Heir to Nothing — A dying lord names the party in his will — they inherit a castle, its debts, and the three siblings who expected to.
The Cartographer's Lie — A famous map shows a town that no one can find. The mapmaker is paid to keep it on the map; ask why.
Borrowed Faces — People in a border town are waking up as strangers — same body, wrong life. The town clerk has the only ledger that still matches.
The Bell That Wasn't Rung — A city's warning bell tolled at midnight, but the watch swears no one touched it. Three people left town before dawn.
Salt for the Dead — A coastal hamlet salts its dead and buries them facing the sea. One grave is empty and the tide is coming in.
The Debt Collector's Apprentice — A devil's junior clerk has lost the contract for a soul due this week and will pay handsomely to get it back — quietly.
Wolves in the Walls — A noble house hires exterminators. The 'rats' in the walls speak, and they're paying the party's rivals to look the other way.
The Last Performance — A traveling opera arrives in town. Anyone who watches the final act forgets the day they saw it — and the troupe never ages.
Inheritance of Teeth — A jeweler dies and leaves a locked box to 'whoever can open it without greed.' Everyone who's tried has lost a tooth.
The Drought Merchant — A stranger sells rain in bottles, and the wells go dry the week he arrives in any town. He's three towns ahead of a mob.
Quiet on the Mountain — A monastery has gone silent. Pilgrims who climb up don't come down, but smoke still rises from the kitchen each morning.
The Understudy King — The king has a double for dangerous events. The double is doing a better job, and someone has noticed the original is missing.
Coins from the River — Gold coins keep washing up downstream, all minted by a kingdom that fell two centuries ago. The current runs the wrong way.
A Funeral Without a Body — A grieving widow hires the party to attend her husband's funeral and watch the crowd. He's not dead — he's in the crowd.
The Lending Library — A library lends any book ever written, due in seven days. A patron is three days overdue on a book that shouldn't exist.
Frost in High Summer — One farmstead is locked in winter while the valley bakes. The family inside set a table for guests who never left.
The Honest Thief — A burglar returns everything he steals with a note naming who really owns it. Three of his 'corrections' have started a feud.
Marrow & Mortar — A new bridge is finished ahead of schedule and under budget. The mason used bone in the mortar, and the bone remembers.
The Sleeping Court — An entire noble court sleeps and won't wake. The cook is awake, has been for a month, and refuses to say what she saw.
Two Moons, One Night — For one night, a second moon will rise. A cult, a sage, and a smuggler all want the party somewhere different when it does.
The Refund — A retired adventurer wants to return a cursed item to the wizard who sold it — and the shop has been boarded up for years.
Wages of the Pit — A mining town pays better than any other and never advertises. The deepest shaft has a door, and the door has a lock on the inside.
The Matchmaker's Ledger — A matchmaker's pairings always last — because she trades a year of each marriage to something that collects in person.
Echoes in the Archive — A scribe is being blackmailed with a confession he hasn't written yet. The letters arrive the day before he'd send them.
The Greenest Field — One farmer's crops never fail. His neighbors are vanishing one by one, and his field grows a little wider each time.
Passage for the Penniless — A ferryman takes the poor across for free. They arrive as someone else's memory, and the rich are starting to envy them.
The Unsent Army — A general drills troops for a war that ended a decade ago. Someone is still paying them, and the pay is real.
Glass in the Garden — A noblewoman's roses are turning to glass. She'll pay to stop it, but she's the one watering them with tears she can't explain.
The Counterfeit Saint — A village's miracle-working relic is a fake — but it still works, and the real one wants to know who's wearing its name.
Dead Man's Tab — A tavern keeps a tab for a regular who died last winter. Someone keeps drinking it down, and the keeper is too scared to refuse.
The Migrating Door — A door stands in a field, leading nowhere. Each dawn it's a mile closer to town, and last night someone walked out of it.
Heirloom Weather — A family heirloom controls the local weather. The heir is selling it to a foreigner, and the valley's farmers just found out.
The Apology Tour — A reformed warlord travels the lands he ruined, paying restitution. Three of his old lieutenants want him silenced first.
Names in the Snow — Names appear in fresh snowfall each winter — a list of who'll die that season. This year, a party member's name is on it.
The Borrowed Year — A child in a sickbed ages a year each night while a healthy stranger in town grows a year younger. They've never met.
Low Tide Market — A market appears on the seabed at the lowest tide of the year, selling drowned things. The tide is lower than ever this time.
The Unfinished Symphony — A composer died mid-work; the orchestra plays the finished half nightly. When they play the rest, the dead will stand to listen.
Wardens of the Empty Vault — A guild guards a vault that holds nothing — and pays triple to anyone who'll swear it holds nothing. The auditors are coming.
The Generous Plague — A sickness sweeps the city, but the afflicted grow kinder, wiser, calmer. The temple wants it cured before anyone asks why.
Stones That Wander — A ring of standing stones is one stone short each morning. The missing stones are being found in people's bedrooms, warm to the touch.
The Reluctant Oracle — A child speaks prophecies in her sleep. Her parents charge admission; the prophecies have started naming the paying customers.
Letters to the Living — The post office delivers letters from the dead — accurate, dated, and signed. The postmaster reads them all first.
The Caged Storm — A collector keeps a thunderstorm in a birdcage. It's learning the layout of his house, and it's patient.
Heir of the Drowned City — A beggar claims to be heir to a sunken kingdom and can prove it. Three nations would rather the proof never reach a court.
The Quiet Quarter — One city district has gone perfectly, eerily polite. The watch won't patrol it, and the people who move in never move out.
Bread and Circuses — A baker's bread makes the town docile and content. The mayor knows, approves, and has just placed a much larger order.
The Returning Comet — A comet returns after a century, and so does everyone who was born under it last time — at the age they were when it left.
Hollow Harvest — Scarecrows are appearing in fields that have no farmer. They face the village, and each week there's one more of them.
The Final Client — An assassin wants to hire the party to stop their own last contract — the target is the assassin, and the buyer is a mirror.

shopNames.name: Shop & Merchant Names
items: The Bent Nail — carpentry & joinery — Every cabinet has a hidden drawer, free of charge; the carpenter keeps a ledger of what clients hide and has never once read it, she swears.
Mistress Vell's Remedies — apothecary — Cures what ails you, and the back shelf cures what ails someone else. She requires a name for the second kind.
The Gilded Scale — moneylender & exchange — Fair rates, iron vault, and a polite refusal to explain why the scale itself is chained to the floor.
Harrow & Sons — undertakers — There are no sons. There never were. Mr. Harrow has been 'the son' for four generations and looks remarkably fresh on it.
The Patient Anvil — blacksmith — No rush orders, no exceptions. The one blade she ever hurried is the one the city still tells stories about.
Quince's Curiosities — oddments & antiques — Everything is genuine, nothing is what the label says, and Quince will happily explain the difference for the price of a rumor.
The Wandering Needle — tailor — Garments altered while you wait; the needle works alone after closing, and the tailor pays it in thread and privacy.
Bram's Provisions — general goods — The dried rations never spoil and nobody can find the supplier; Bram inherited the contract and is terrified of meeting them.
The Seventh Lock — locksmith — Six apprentice grades, and a seventh door in the workshop the master opens only to refuse new commissions.
Inkwell & Owl — stationer & scribe — Letters written, contracts copied, and — after dark, for old clients — handwriting matched to any sample you bring.
The Hollow Wheel — cartwright — Wagons built with a smuggler's compartment as standard; the guild fined him once, then quietly placed a bulk order.
Saffron House — spice merchant — The saffron is real; the pepper is cut with something that makes customers oddly agreeable, which is why the magistrate shops here.
Greaves & Glory — armorer — Dented champion's plate hangs unsold in the window; the owner buys back every piece she's ever sold to the dead.
The Mended Drum — instrument maker — Repairs anything with strings or skin; the drum above the door belonged to an army that surrendered when it stopped.
Pellam's Maps & Charts — cartographer — Sells two versions of every map: the accurate one, and the one the harbormaster insists tourists receive.
The Sugared Tooth — confectioner — Candies cure homesickness for exactly one hour; the recipe calls for an ingredient she'll only gather during funerals.
Old Cordwain — cobbler — Boots resoled overnight by someone Cordwain refuses to name; payment left out in a saucer like for a cat.
The Brazen Kettle — coppersmith — Kettles that whistle warnings — not when water boils, but when someone in the room lies.
Nightsoil & Daisies — gardener's supply — The compost is municipal, the daisies are spectacular, and the proprietor knows what every garden in the city is burying.
The Counting Crow — pawnshop — Lends on anything, never sells the unclaimed — the back room is a museum of the city's worst years, catalogued by heartbreak.
Verro Brothers — glassblowers — One brother blows glass you can't break; the other blows glass that breaks on command. They no longer speak, and share one furnace.
The Last Candle — chandler — Tapers that burn precisely one conversation long; the temple buys gross lots and won't say for which rite.
Hessa's Hides — tanner & leatherworks — Leather from beasts most tanners refuse; she pays hunters double and asks them to stop describing the animals.
The Modest Crown — jeweler — Specializes in paste replicas for nobles who've quietly sold the originals — discretion priced higher than the gems ever were.
Furrow & Field — seed merchant — Seeds true to label except the unmarked jar, which grows whatever the buyer most needs and bills them accordingly.
The Iron Page — bookbinder — Bindings that lock, scream, or forget; bring your own book, and don't ask about the shelf of volumes still waiting for owners to return.
Calloway's Strings — luthier — Fiddles tuned to rooms, not notes; the one hanging in the window plays itself when its maker's name is spoken.
The Honest Bushel — grocer — Scales certified by three guilds; the honesty is real, which is why half the market pays him to weigh disputes instead of vegetables.
Smoke & Ember — pipe shop — Blends for memory, courage, and sleep; the proprietor's own pipe is never lit, and regulars know better than to offer.
The Crooked Florin — gambling supplies — Honest dice and marked ones, clearly labeled and identically priced — 'the house margin,' he says, 'is knowing which you bought.'
Marrow's Fine Meats — butcher — The best cuts in the district, and a standing midnight order, paid in old coin, that Marrow preps blindfolded by family tradition.
The Glass Garden — florist — Flowers preserved in glass at their peak moment; she takes commissions to preserve other peak moments, and her terms are strange.
Tindersworth & Co. — lamp & oil — Streetlamp contract holder for forty years; the unlit lamp on Wren Lane stays dark by agreement with something that pays better than the city.
The Folded Crane — paper goods — Paper birds that deliver messages within the city walls — one copper each, two if the recipient is hiding.
Grist & Stone — miller's storefront — Flour ground at the old tide-mill; loaves from it rise double on the night of a drowning, which the bakers' guild tracks but won't discuss.
The Velvet Muzzle — exotic animal dealer — Licensed for songbirds and lizards; the muffled crate room is 'awaiting paperwork,' permanently.
Aldous & Aldous — solicitors and notaries — The brass plate lists two names; clients see one man who answers comfortably to both, depending on which side of the contract he's arguing.
The Whetted Edge — knife grinder — Pushcart by day, shopfront by night; he grinds free for the city watch and remembers every blade he's ever sharpened — and for whom.
Bellamy's Baths — bathhouse & barber — Steam, gossip, and a razor that's shaved three kings; the gossip is the actual product, sold by subscription.
The Quiet Loom — weaver — Cloth that muffles footsteps, woven on a loom that makes no sound; the thieves' guild and the temple choir are both standing customers.
Pickle & Pot — preserves & pickles — Jars sealed with wax stamps of the year's events; collectors buy vintage years for the stamps, and one year is banned from sale.
The Standing Stone — mason's yard — Headstones carved in advance from dreams the mason can't refuse; the yard's back row is for people who haven't died yet.
Wick's Clockworks — clockmaker — Clocks that keep the owner's time, not the city's; the magistrate's runs eleven minutes fast, which has decided three trials.
The Salted Rose — perfumery — Scents bottled from places — 'harbor at dawn,' 'the king's funeral,' 'your childhood kitchen.' The last one costs the most and she always gets it right.
Dunmore's Rope & Rigging — chandlery — Rope guaranteed to hold; every coil sold with a knot already tied in the end that Dunmore asks you never to untie.
The Cartographer's Widow — used goods — Sells her late husband's effects, one item per customer, and somehow always has exactly one item left.
Fletch & Feather — bowyer — Arrows fletched from molted feathers of the rookery at Crowsperch; they fly true but occasionally report back.
The Mortar's Daughter — alchemical supply — Reagents weighed exactly, no questions — questions cost extra, answers cost more, and silence about your purchase is the only thing that's free.
Hobb's Sundries — everything store — Cramped shelves where customers always find one item they didn't ask for but need within the week; Hobb stocks by intuition and refuses returns on prophecy.
The Tided Chest — salvage & maritime goods — Everything reclaimed from wrecks, blessed twice, and priced by how badly the sea wanted to keep it.
